#   Foreword 

 Computer Science as a subject never stands still.   Teaching it can often feel like trying to keep pace with a discipline that is constantly reinventing itself.   In recent years, the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence has accelerated this challenge even further.   AI has, in many respects, made teaching computer science both easier and more difficult than ever before.   Easier, due to the tools available to teachers and students being extraordinarily powerful.   More difficult, because those same tools can obscure the very fundamentals we are trying to teach. 

 In the classroom, it is not enough to simply introduce students to programming languages and frameworks.   We must help them navigate an ecosystem where AI-assisted development is commonplace.   Students will experiment with code-generating tools and lean on these when the going gets tough.   They may rely on them to produce working solutions before they fully understand variables, program flow, or the techniques used.   While this can accelerate progress, it often leaves students unable to explain why their code works.   As educators, our responsibility is to ensure students do not mistake correct output for genuine understanding. 

 Mark Price’s .NET books have been a popular addition to Greenhead College’s programming book library.   His books are structured in a way that respects the learner’s journey, carefully scaffolding concepts while still engaging with modern, real-world development practices.   Clear explanations, well-chosen examples, and a strong emphasis on building understanding step by step have made his books some of the most reliable resources I have used in both introductory and intermediate programming courses.   They have proven particularly effective in supporting students through substantial coursework projects, where confidence and clarity matter just as much as technical correctness. 

 With the rise of AI-assisted development, the landscape is shifting again.   The question is no longer should students use AI tools, but how can they use them responsibly and effectively.   This is why a book like  * Web Dev with an AI Sidekick *  feels so timely.   Rather than ignoring AI or treating it as a shortcut, the book directly addresses the tension educators now face: how to embrace these tools while ensuring they enhance learning instead of replacing it. 

 My expectation for this book is that it will bring the same strengths that have defined Mark Price’s previous work.   If AI is approached with the same measured and thoughtful mindset that he has applied to frameworks and languages throughout his writing, this book will help students develop not only functional solutions, but real understanding.   That balance, between capability and comprehension, is exactly what educators and learners need in this new era of software development. 

* Stephen Wood *

* Head of Computer Science at Greenhead College *

#   Preface 

* Web Dev with an AI Sidekick *  reinvents how beginners learn to code by harnessing the power of interactive AI.   This comprehensive guide transforms the static textbook experience into a two-way conversation with your AI coding partner.   Instead of just reading about code, you’ll prompt an AI to explain concepts, generate examples, and help you solve problems on the fly.   It’s like having a tutor available 24/7. 

 The result is a highly engaging learning journey that adapts to your questions and needs.   You can ask the “dumb” questions without fear, get instant clarifications, and receive step-by-step guidance tailored to your pace.   It’s an engaging way to learn programming fast, making coding more accessible and rewarding.   By leveraging AI models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and others, the book turns the latest AI technology into your personal coding mentor and collaborator. 

#   Who this book is for 

 This book is for complete beginners who are curious about web development and excited about what’s possible using AI to both learn programming skills and build complete projects.   This book is ideal for: 

*    Students exploring coding for the first time 
*    Career changers entering the technology field and needing a friendly entry point 
*    Self-taught learners who feel overwhelmed by traditional textbooks or video courses 
*    Creatives, designers, or writers who want to build interactive web projects 
*    Hobbyists or entrepreneurs with app ideas but no formal training 
*    Anyone fascinated by AI and wondering how it can help them learn to code 

 It especially appeals to people who prefer hands-on, practical learning and value being able to ask questions in natural language while coding. 

##   What prerequisites do you need? 

 None.   The book assumes zero prior experience in programming, web development, or using AI tools.   If you can open a browser and follow instructions, you’re ready.   The early chapters walk through every step, including how to sign up for ChatGPT, install VS Code with various extensions like GitHub Copilot, and even how to talk to an AI effectively.   Later, the book explains how web pages are structured and styled, how to draw graphics, what a variable is, what a loop is, and even how to host your finished web projects.   It builds up from nothing to a complete website. 

##   Why should you buy this book? 

 This book teaches modern web development faster, more enjoyably, and more interactively than any traditional book. 

 It introduces a fun and friendly way to learn by using AI tools as a tutor, debugger, and coding assistant. 

 It’s tailored for beginners like you, removing jargon and gatekeeping. 

 It covers everything in one book: frontend, backend, databases, deployment, and development tools. 

 It delivers real-world results.   You will build and deploy a fully functional web app. 

 It keeps you up-to-date by teaching you how to learn continuously with AI.   It’s not just a reference book about specific syntax. 

 It’s future-proof because you gain both web development skills and fluency with AI-assisted development, a major advantage in today’s job market. 

#   What this book covers 

 Let’s briefly review what you can expect in this book. 

##   Part 1: Frontend Web Development 

 Part 1 introduces the main technologies used to build the visible parts of a web page in dedicated chapters, each structured for interactive learning.   You’ll start with the building blocks of the Web: HTML and CSS with SVG for graphics, then progress to JavaScript and its typed superset TypeScript. 

 Every chapter introduces core concepts in a friendly way and immediately invites you to put them into practice by chatting with an AI.   For example, when learning HTML, you’ll ask the AI to generate a simple web page structure and then tweak it through prompts.   This way, you get to experience firsthand that HTML defines the meaning and structure. 

 In the CSS chapter, you will style the page and see how CSS controls layout, colors, spacing, and typography, reinforcing that CSS describes how elements should be rendered on screen, on paper, or on other media. 

 JavaScript brings your web pages to life as you collaborate with the AI to make your pages interactive, reflecting JavaScript’s role as a core web language, and TypeScript is introduced as an extension that adds static types to JavaScript for safer coding. 

 Each chapter includes exercises where you ask an AI tool to explain, revise, or debug small examples.   Each chapter wraps up with a quiz to solidify your knowledge, and a curated list of official documentation links for further reference, encouraging you to consult authoritative sources as part of your learning. 

##   Part 2: Backend Web Development 

 We then cover all the essential backend web development technologies, again in dedicated chapters, each structured for interactive learning.   You’ll explore database interactions with SQL, dive into programming with Python, master web frameworks with Django, and get comfortable with command line scripting for automation with Bash. 

 By the end of  * Part 1 *  and  * Part 2 *  , you will have a solid grasp of the entire web stack, from frontend to backend, all gained through hands-on, interactive practice with an AI chatbot by your side. 

##   Part 3: Survey Project 

 Now armed with the fundamentals, you’ll embark on an exciting capstone project: developing a survey creation web application using Django, modern web technologies, and your AI assistant at every step.   This part of the book is a project-based tutorial split into several chapters that mirror a real development workflow. 

 In the planning phase, you’ll design the app’s features and data models in Django with the AI helping brainstorm model fields and relationships.   We’ll set up a professional development environment using Docker containers to run Django and a database locally, ensuring that everyone can follow along with the same setup. 

 The book provides detailed instructions for using either OpenAI Codex or Anthropic Claude Code, cutting-edge AI-powered coding environments, to build the project.   We’ll show how Codex or Claude Code seamlessly integrates AI into the coding workflow, so you can write code using instructions and use the AI to draft code while you review, test, and revise it.   Through this AI-enhanced process, you’ll implement all the key features of the survey app: 

*    Creating surveys with multiple question types (text, multiple-choice, ratings, and so on.) 
*    Letting users submit responses. 
*    Building an admin interface for managing surveys. 
*    Displaying results in dynamic tables and charts. 

 Along the way, you’ll practice AI-assisted debugging and testing: for instance, writing unit tests for your Django views. 

 We emphasize effective prompt techniques to get useful output from the AI, and also caution about AI quirks and how to verify and correct AI-generated solutions. 

 The project chapters also highlight collaboration between tools.   For example, using Git version control with GitHub or locally to manage changes suggested by the AI, and using Docker for local live testing. 

 In the final project chapter, we guide you through deploying the finished app to a production environment.   Throughout deployment, the AI copilot can assist with tasks like writing Dockerfiles or  ` .gitignore `  files. 

 By the end of  * Part 3 *  , you will have built a full-stack web application and practiced using AI tools during planning, coding, testing, and deployment.   This is a portfolio-worthy project that reinforces everything you learned in  * Part 1 *  and  * Part 2 *  and teaches you how those pieces interconnect in a real app. 

 More importantly, you will have experienced a new paradigm of building software: coding with an AI partner. 

##   AI-interactive philosophy 

 Unique to this book is its AI-interactive philosophy.   The content stays fresh and up-to-date because instead of relying on pre-written text alone, it leverages real-time AI models that are continually improving.   Whenever a new API emerges or a language update happens, your AI copilot can fill you in making this a book that grows with the technology. 

 We also stress good habits, like cross-checking AI outputs against official documentation.   Each chapter directs you to the primary sources, like the official Python docs and Django’s docs, so you learn to verify and deepen your knowledge beyond what the AI provides. 

 The tone and content of this book is tailored for complete beginners and written in plain, friendly US English.   Complex topics are broken down into manageable, conversational exchanges with the AI, making the learning experience feel more like a guided dialogue than a lecture. 

 The book is about learning a new way to code, one where you ask the AI to teach you concepts and why things work and then apply that knowledge creatively. 

 Whether you’re a student, a professional looking to switch careers, or just tech-curious,  * Web Dev with an AI Sidekick *  will fast-track your journey from novice to confident web developer. 

 By the final page, you’ll not only have a functioning web app deployed online, but also the know-how to keep learning any new technology with the help of your AI sidekick. 

#   Our principles for using AI-generated content 

 This book was written by Mark J.   Price.   Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude were used to help explore ideas, troubleshoot code, and generate examples during development.   This thoughtful use of AI reflects the book’s core philosophy that learning to code can be more intuitive, responsive, and engaging when guided by interactive AI. 

 The purpose behind incorporating AI in the writing process was to offer readers more examples across a wider range of programming languages, cover solutions in greater depth, and address new scenarios more quickly. 

 All the instructional content in this book were developed, reviewed, and tested by the author and Packt’s editorial team.   Packt does not publish AI-generated content as a substitute for expert authorship.

##   Conventions used 

 There are a number of text conventions used throughout this book. 

` CodeInText `  : Indicates code words in text, database table names, folder names, filenames, file extensions, pathnames, dummy URLs, user input, and Twitter handles.   For example: “Change the  ` <h1> `  and  ` <title> `  text to something else.” 

 A block of code is set as follows: 

```
<p>
  HTML tells the browser what each piece of content <em>is</em>.
  Styling comes later (that's CSS), and interactivity comes later (that's JavaScript).
</p>
```

 When we wish to draw your attention to a particular part of a code block, the relevant lines or items are set in bold: 

```
<h2>Useful link</h2>
<p>
  Here's a link to learn more about HTML:
  <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML">MDN Web Docs: HTML</a>.
</p>
```

 Any command-line input or output is written as follows: 

```
code --install-extension ms-vscode.live-server
```

** Bold **  : Indicates a new term, an important word, or words that you see on the screen.   For instance, words in menus or dialog boxes appear in the text like this.   For example: “In VS Code, click    the  ** Extensions **  icon or navigate to  ** View **  |  ** Extensions **  .”

#   Breaking down the chapters of this book 

 Let’s start by breaking down what you will learn in the rest of the chapters of this book.   After this first chapter, the book is divided into three major parts: 

1.  ** Frontend Web Development **  : Learn the technologies for developing what the user experiences in their web browser: HTML, CSS, SVG, JavaScript, and TypeScript. 
2.  ** Backend Web Development **  : Learn the technologies for developing the parts of a website that run on the web server: a SQL database, Python, Django, and Bash, aka shell scripting for automating developer tasks. 
3.  ** Survey Project **  : Build and then optionally deploy a complete website for creating, taking, and analyzing surveys and polls. 

##   Frontend Web Development 

[* Chapter 2 *](#02.xhtml#_idTextAnchor098)  ,  * HTML – Structuring Your Web Pages *  , covers the basics of HTML (HyperText Markup Language).   You’ll use the AI to generate a simple page and, in doing so, learn about elements, tags, and attributes.   You’ll learn about HTML’s role in defining web content structure (from headings to links and images).   You will create a contact form, introducing form elements. 

[* Chapter 3 *](#03.xhtml#_idTextAnchor154)  ,  * CSS – Styling Your Web Pages *  , shows you how to control presentation and layout.   You will get the AI to explain selectors, properties, and values.   You will apply styles to your web page from  [* Chapter 2 *](#02.xhtml#_idTextAnchor098)  ,  * HTML – Structuring Your Web Pages *  .    You will learn about responsive design and making mobile-friendly web pages using CSS media queries. 

[* Chapter 4 *](#04.xhtml#_idTextAnchor212)  ,  * SVG – Drawing Scalable Graphics *  , introduces SVG as a way to generate graphics with code, which will be useful for charting survey results.   AI will explain that SVG is an XML-based markup language for 2D graphics and how it differs from canvas/bitmaps.   Through AI-guided examples, you create basic shapes (circle, rectangle, line) in SVG and embed them in HTML. 

[* Chapter 5 *](#05.xhtml#_idTextAnchor266)  ,  * JavaScript – Making Web Pages Interactive *  , covers fundamental JavaScript concepts like variables, functions, events, and the DOM.   We start by describing what JavaScript is (a lightweight, interpreted language that runs in browsers) and where to include  ` <script> `  blocks in HTML. 

[* Chapter 6 *](#06.xhtml#_idTextAnchor316)  ,  * TypeScript – Safer JavaScript *  , introduces TypeScript as a superset of JavaScript that adds static types and explains why they are useful. 

##   Backend Web Development 

[* Chapter 7 *](#07.xhtml#_idTextAnchor374)  ,  * SQL – Managing Data *  , demystifies SQL (using SQLite and a simple database for practice).   The AI explains what a database is and how SQL is used to query data.   You will practice basic SQL commands through AI prompts:  ` SELECT `  statements, filtering (  ` WHERE `  ), and sorting (  ` ORDER BY `  ).   The AI can generate a sample dataset (like a  ` users `  table) and challenge you with queries (“How would you get all users who signed up this month?”). 

[* Chapter 8 *](#08.xhtml#_idTextAnchor494)  ,  * Python – Programming on the Backend *  , covers fundamental Python syntax and concepts, preparing readers for backend web development.   You’ll install Python and then learn coding for Python basics like variables, loops, and functions.   You will ask the AI to explain code line by line, reinforcing understanding. 

[* Chapter 9 *](#09.xhtml#_idTextAnchor598)  ,  * Django – Web Development on the Backend *  , focuses on Django, Python’s most commonly-used web framework.   Your AI will explain how Django works with its  ** MVT **  (  ** Model-View-Template **  ) pattern, which is related to but distinct from the traditional  ** MVC **  (  ** Model-View-Controller **  ) pattern, and why it’s used for rapid web development.   With AI guidance, you start a Django project (the book provides step-by-step instructions, and the AI can help troubleshoot).   You’ll create a new Django project, which lays the groundwork for the full project in the  * Survey Project *  part of the book.   The AI helps you write a simple view and a template.   You learn how Django serves HTML and how to use template variables. 

[* Chapter 10 *](#10.xhtml#_idTextAnchor689)  ,  * Bash/Shell – Command-Line Skills for Developers *  , briefly steps aside from web programming to teach Bash/Shell usage, since many development tasks involve the command line, especially to automate deployments.   You will practice common commands (  ` ls `  ,  ` cd `  ,  ` mkdir `  ,  ` rm `  , etc.) by having the AI describe what each does and trying them in a terminal or emulator.   The AI will walk you through creating a small Bash/Shell script to automate a task like backing up a file or starting your Django server. 

##   Survey Project 

[* Chapter 11 *](#11.xhtml#_idTextAnchor764)  ,  * Setting Up Your Project Environment *  , kicks off the TallyApp survey project and configures tools.   You will see an overview of the survey app you’ll build and its features, like creating surveys, taking surveys, and viewing results.   Step-by-step instructions (with screenshots or code snippets) for setting up VS Code with GitHub Copilot are provided.   You will be introduced to a Docker-based development environment and how to place code under version control using Git. 

[* Chapter 12 *](#12.xhtml#_idTextAnchor809)  ,  * Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Testing *  , teaches you how to design and implement a layered testing strategy for TallyApp, write meaningful unit and integration tests in Django, automate real browser interactions with end-to-end tests using Playwright, and use AI tools to generate tests automatically. 

[* Chapter 13 *](#13.xhtml#_idTextAnchor872)  ,  * Specifying and Building the Initial Project *  , defines a clear project brief for TallyApp, translates that into an actionable development plan, guides you to scaffold a Django 6 project with appropriate apps and models, and implements core authentication and survey functionality. 

[* Chapter 14 *](#14.xhtml#_idTextAnchor922)  ,  * Adding Project Features Using Spec-Driven Development *  , covers how to implement a structured feature specification, use an AI coding assistant to implement it inside an existing Django project, and verify that the implementation satisfies clearly defined acceptance criteria. 

[* Chapter 15 *](#15.xhtml#_idTextAnchor977)  ,  * Deploying to Public Servers *  , reviews options for deploying TallyApp to a server connected to the wider internet so that members of the public can use the website.   You will deploy TallyApp to a publicly accessible server, understand how requests flow through a production Django stack, know how to preserve and back up user data across deployments, and know what has to change as traffic and expectations increase. 

* Epilogue *  , reviews the next steps on your web development learning journey. 

* Appendix *  , contains answers to questions at the end of each chapter. 

##   Why these languages and skills? 

 You might wonder why I’ve chosen to cover these specific languages, frameworks, and skills.   One major reason is that Stack Overflow conducts a survey of thousands of developers every year and one question they ask is:  * Which programming, scripting, and markup languages have you done extensive development work in over the past year? *

 The 31,771 responses to this question in the 2025 survey revealed the top six languages that developers reported using extensively over the past year are JavaScript, HTML/CSS, SQL, Python, Bash/Shell, and TypeScript, as shown in  * Figure 1.1 *  : 

![](Images/B34553_01_01.png)

 Figure 1.1: 2025 survey of the most extensively used programming languages 

 You can see these results in the survey at the following link:  [  https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology#most-popular-technologies-language  ](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology#most-popular-technologies-language)

 These results make sense when you realize that all those languages are needed to do web development, and most programming work these days is web development.   All that’s missing in the top six are SVG for drawing scalable vector graphics, and Django which is the most popular web development framework for Python.   I even briefly considered naming the book,  * Top Six Programming Languages *  , but ultimately decided that web development is a better connecting theme for a book that covers all those languages. 

 You can see a summary of what roles each of the languages and frameworks play in web development in  * Figure 1.2 *  : 

![](Images/B34553_01_02.png)

 Figure 1.2: Language, framework, and tool roles in web development 

##   How to use this book 

 Technical books are not meant to be read in a strictly linear way.   Unlike a novel, you are free to move around based on your interests, your goals, and your existing experience.   Some readers will feel an immediate pull toward building a complete project and may be tempted to jump ahead to the later chapters where that work comes together. 

 That instinct is understandable, and I encourage you to explore.   However, if you do, you will quickly encounter the practical reality that web development draws on multiple layers of knowledge.   Concepts that may seem slow or isolated in earlier chapters become important to understand when combined in a real application.   The structure of this book reflects that progression. 

 As you’ve seen in the chapter breakdown, the first two parts of the book focus on learning individual technologies one at a time.   This is deliberate.   Each language, framework, and tool is introduced in isolation so you can understand its role, its strengths, and how it behaves without unnecessary complexity.   Trying to learn everything at once often leads to confusion and shallow understanding.   Learning one tool at a time makes the later project less confusing. 

 The final part of the book brings these elements together into a complete project.   This is where the earlier investment pays off.   Instead of copying and pasting code without context, you will be more likely to understand what you are building and why it works the way it does. 

 It is also important to recognize that a book is only one part of the learning process.   Real progress comes from a combination of reading, hands-on practice, experimentation, and exposure to different perspectives.   It would be impossible to write a single book that teaches everything about web development.   And most readers learn more thoroughly from a variety of instructional techniques.   Videos, documentation, and community discussions all play a role.   Most importantly, your own persistence and curiosity will determine how far you go. 

 Learning to build software is a long-term effort.   It requires time, repetition, and patience.   This book is designed to give you structure so that your time is well spent.   Instead of piecing together dozens of free but disconnected tutorials and articles, you are following a coherent path where each chapter builds on the last. 

 Approach the material in a way that works for you, but understand why the book is organized this way.   If you take the time to build a solid foundation, the later stages will feel far more rewarding and far less frustrating.

#   Setting up your web development environment 

 Before    you start programming, you’ll need a code editor for multiple languages including, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL, and Python, either from Microsoft or a third party.   I recommend VS Code because it supports extensions for all common languages and runs cross-platform on Windows, Mac, and Linux. 

 VS Code    is by far the most popular code editor or IDE across all developers with over 75% of professional developers    selecting it in a Stack Overflow 2025 survey, which you can read at the following link:  [  https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology/#1-dev-id-es  ](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology/#1-dev-id-es)  .
