 Now that you have set up your development environment, let’s dive into how to get the best out of an AI chatbot when you want it to act as your coach for learning web development. 

#   Learning with an AI chatbot as your coach 

 AI chatbots    like ChatGPT    can be useful learning tools when you use them well. 

 This section compares three chatbots that are commonly used for learning web development. 

** Good practice **  : If you are new to web development or unsure which tools to choose, use the following setup.   This is the simplest path through the book, and what the examples assume: 

*   ** Chatbot **  : ChatGPT (free or Plus at $20 USD per month) 
*   ** Code editor or IDE **  : VS Code (free) 
*   ** IDE-integrated coding assistant **  : GitHub    Copilot (individual plans like Copilot Free and Copilot Pro include GitHub AI Credits    allowances that vary by plan) 
*   ** Command-line coding assistant **  : OpenAI    Codex (because it’s currently included with    ChatGPT Plus) 

 You can complete this entire book using just these tools.   Other options like Claude or Gemini are excellent, and you are encouraged to explore them later.   But switching tools too early can feel overwhelming and slow down your learning.   Start simple, build confidence, and then experiment. 

 Now let’s compare chatbots: OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini. 

##   OpenAI’s ChatGPT 

 ChatGPT is    particularly useful for explanations, debugging help, and iterative back-and-forth while you learn.   When you’re stuck on HTML semantics, JavaScript quirks, or Django data model logic, a well-structured prompt will usually produce a useful explanation. 

 Free vs paid subscriptions: 

*   ** Free **  : The free version    works well for conversational learning but does not include access to Codex coding agent. 
*   ** Go ($8 USD per month) **  : Expanded access with more messages, uploads, image creation, and longer memory. 
*   ** Plus ($20 USD per month) **  : Access to advanced GPT family models, which are generally better at reasoning, code generation, and maintaining context across longer sessions.   Access to Codex coding agent, projects, and custom GPTs.   This is my recommendation if you want more capability without committing to a high monthly cost. 
*   ** Pro ($100 USD per month) **  : 5x more usage than Plus with the Frontier Pro model, maximum access to Codex and deep research, and unlimited and faster image creation. 
*   ** Business ($20 USD per month per seat) / Enterprise **  : Best for corporate teams because it requires 2+ seats billed annually.   OpenAI promises that your data will never be used for training their models. 

 ChatGPT pricing    information can be found at the following link:  [  https://chatgpt.com/pricing/  ](https://chatgpt.com/pricing/%20)

 All major AI providers offer a range of models that trade speed and cost for capability.   While the names differ, the pattern is consistent.   OpenAI names its faster, less-thinking models  ` mini `  .   For example,  ` GPT-5 mini `  .   Google names its Gemini faster, less-thinking models Flash, and its deeper thinking models Ultra. 

 The current version of the GPT model at the time of writing is 5.5, released on April 23, 2026.   You can learn about GPT-5.5    at the following link:  [  https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-5-5/  ](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-5-5/)  .   OpenAI released version 5.4 on March 5, so improvements happen fast.   Check OpenAI’s releases page for the latest:  [  https://openai.com/research/index/release/  ](https://openai.com/research/index/release/%20)

 How to set it up for success: 

*    Start each session with context by mentioning your stack (HTML, JavaScript, Django, and so on) and your exact goal. 
*    Include instructions like “show clear examples” and “explain line by line.” 
*    Upload smaller files when you want the bot to read and comment on your code. 
*    If you upgrade, explore Custom GPTs via the GPT Store to create a tailored tutor that knows specific development technologies deeply. 

 You can sign up for ChatGPT    at the following link:  [  https://chatgpt.com/  ](https://chatgpt.com/)

##   Anthropic’s Claude 

 Claude is particularly good at    reasoning, explanations, and working with long documents. 

 Claude is often the main alternative people try when they want stronger long-form explanations.   It’s widely used by developers, writers, lawyers, and researchers who care about clarity and depth rather than flashy features. 

 Why people like Claude: 

*    Very    strong at explaining complex ideas calmly and clearly 
*    A very large context window.   You can paste entire files, articles, or chapters 
*    Less likely to produce confident but incorrect explanations 

 Downsides: 

*    Slightly more    conservative (meaning behaviorally cautious, not politically conservative) 

 Anthropic designed Claude around  * constitutional AI *  , a system of explicit ethical principles that guide its responses.   This makes it structurally more cautious than models trained mainly on user feedback.   You can read more about this aspect of Claude at the following link:  [  https://deeperinsights.com/ai-review/claude-ai-features-uses-comparison-to-chatgpt/  ](https://deeperinsights.com/ai-review/claude-ai-features-uses-comparison-to-chatgpt/%20)

*    Code output is good, but tends to be more cautious and incremental than ChatGPT when prototyping 
*    If you prefer a    more measured, explanatory style, Claude is a good choice 

 Anthropic offers several versions of Claude, commonly referred to as Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus.   These are not completely different systems; they are different trade-offs between speed, cost, and capability. 

 A simple way to think about them is: 

*    Haiku for speed 
*    Sonnet for everyday work 
*    Opus for the hardest problems 

 Most beginners should start with Sonnet and only switch when they have a clear reason.   If the task is simple or repetitive, try Haiku.   If the task is complex, unclear, or keeps failing, move up to Opus. 

 Do not treat model choice as a permanent decision.   Pick the model that suits the job. 

 You can sign up for    Claude at the following link:  [  https://claude.ai/  ](https://claude.ai/)

##   Google’s Gemini 

 Gemini has    improved since its initial release and is now competitive with ChatGPT and Claude for many web development tasks. 

 Why do people like it: 

*    Strong    multimodal support.   Text, images, documents, screenshots 
*    Good JavaScript and web-related answers 

 Downsides: 

*    Responses    can sometimes feel generic 
*    Still uneven on deep backend or framework-specific questions 

 You can sign up for    Gemini at the following link:  [  https://gemini.google.com/  ](https://gemini.google.com/)

##   Which chatbot to choose? 

 If you want to choose    your preferred chatbot, then I recommend comparing them for a month each to see which you get on with best.   Each has a distinct personality that suits different people. 

 Now that we’ve reviewed the three main chatbots, you can decide which you’d prefer to use to learn about all the languages that we will cover in the  * Frontend Web Development *  and  * Backend Web Development *  parts of this book.   You could even choose another chatbot that I haven’t covered if you wish or use multiple chatbots simultaneously and compare their results.   This can be a useful way to learn, seeing what each chatbot chooses to include in their responses.   If multiple chatbots emphasize the same information, then you can be more reassured that they are giving accurate responses. 

 Early in your learning, consistency matters more than optimization.   Using one simple, widely supported setup will help you focus on concepts instead of tools.   Do not waste the first week comparing tools.   Pick one setup and start learning.   Tools will change quickly, but the way you think about systems and code will last.   Regardless of which chatbot(s) you choose to use as your learning coach, let’s now look at some important points that apply to all AI chatbots. 

##   Getting the most from the book’s suggested prompts 

 Throughout this book, you will see suggested prompts that you can copy and paste into chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude.   These prompts are designed to give you a starting point for exploring a topic further, but how you use them matters as much as the prompt itself. 

 For example, here’s the first suggested prompt for this chapter: 

** Prompt **  : Please give me a checklist to evaluate whether an AI response actually helped me learn web development. 

 In the book’s GitHub repository, I have created pages with all the suggested prompts for each chapter.   For example, you can find the suggested prompts for this chapter at the following link: 

[  https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch01-intro/readme.md  ](https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch01-intro/readme.md%20)

 While writing this book in Spring 2026, I used Gemini with a Pro subscription and its  ** Fast **  model to answer each of the optional prompts, as shown in  * Figure 1.5 *  : 

![](Images/Image4065.png)

 Figure 1.5: Configuring Gemini Pro to use fast responses 

 Although you can view those Gemini Pro responses in the book’s GitHub repository, I strongly recommend that you enter the same (or similar) prompts into your preferred AI chatbot.   Models improve all the time, and it can be interesting to see the differences in responses based on pricing, model, and thinking time. 

###   Use a baseline custom instruction 

 A practical technique is to define a    baseline instruction that is always applied to your prompts.   This is sometimes called a custom instruction, system prompt, or profile context, depending on the tool. 

 Instead of repeating the same guidance every time, you configure the AI once with instructions like: 

```
You are helping me learn web development. I am reading a book titled *Web Dev with an AI Sidekick*.
[about_me]
- Use clear, beginner-friendly explanations
- Prefer simple, maintainable solutions over complex ones
- When writing code, include comments to explain "why"
- Assume I am using SQLite unless told otherwise
- Use good practices for security and performance but don't overcomplicate while I am learning the basics
```

` [about_me] `  must be replaced with relevant information about you.   For example, if you are a student, you might write: 

```
I have done some basic HTML and CSS before, but I have never written any programming languages. I am 16 years old and a high-school student in the USA. I want to pursue a software development role in the future.
```

 Or if you are a career-switcher, you might write: 

```
I am a building contractor who wants to change careers. I know very little about programming, but I have heard that AI can help me build websites by vibe coding. I am eager and willing to study hard to learn something new.
```

 Or if you are a    technologist in a different area, you might write: 

```
I am a .NET backend developer with five years of experience. I am bored with my current position, and there aren't many .NET job opportunities near me. I want to switch to full stack web development with an emphasis on frontend user interface design.
```

 Once set, every prompt you send will automatically include this context. 

###   How to configure this in common tools 

 Each platform provides a slightly different way to do this: 

*   ** ChatGPT **  : Use  ** Custom Instructions **  in settings.   You can define how the assistant should behave and    what it should know about you. 
*   ** Gemini **  : Use    saved prompts or context features (in supported environments) to establish consistent instructions. 
*   ** Claude **  : Use  ** Projects **  or conversation setup instructions to define persistent context for a session    or workspace. 

 The names differ, but the idea is the same: set your expectations once, reuse them everywhere. 

##   AI magnifies whatever habits you already have 

 AI does not make you good at web development.   It makes you more of whatever you already are: 

*    If you understand fundamentals, AI multiplies your output 
*    If you hand-wave fundamentals, AI multiplies your confusion 

 For example: AI can generate code, but it cannot know whether that code matches how you think the code should work unless you do. 

 For example, let’s take HTML.   If you already think in terms of document structure, accessibility, and semantic meaning, then AI can speed you up dramatically. 

 You could enter the following prompt: 

```
Generate a semantic HTML layout for a blog page with header, nav, main content, and aside. 
```

 When you review the response from the AI, you immediately understand: 

*    Why  ` <main> `  exists 
*    Why  ` <article> `  vs  ` <section> `  matters 
*    Where the mistakes are 

 You’ll correct any mistakes that the AI has made in seconds. 

 But if you don’t understand semantics, AI will happily produce something that looks right but is structurally wrong.   You won’t notice missing landmarks, broken accessibility, or misuse of headings.   You ship fragile markup and never know why things feel off later.   AI didn’t cause this problem but it did amplify it. 

 If you copy CSS generated by an AI until it looks right, you’ll end up with styling that works only by accident.   Worse, AI will make it faster to reach that broken state. 

 When debugging, if you already read error messages, form hypotheses, and isolate variables, then AI becomes a debugging partner.   You can say: 

```
Here's the error message. What's the most likely cause and how do I confirm it?
```

 You learn faster because you see the reasoning. 

 But if you don’t already know the basic tenets of debugging skills, then AI lets you thrash faster by changing five things at once, you end up pasting fixes blindly, and even creating new bugs!   You feel busy, but you’re not learning. 

** Prompt **  : Please compare learning web development with AI vs without AI.   What skills improve and what skills degrade? 

##   Your learning style 

 If you naturally ask: 

*    Why this pattern? 
*    Why not another? 
*    What breaks if I change this? 

 AI can be patient and available whenever you need to ask another question. 

 But if your instinct is,  * Just give me the solution *  , then AI will happily comply, but you’ll finish projects without understanding them.   Do not let the tool do your thinking for you. 

 You need to use AI as an explainer, a reviewer, a sparring partner in decision making, or a debugger, not as the primary author, architect, or decision maker. 

 Some good phrases to frequently use in your chats with the AI: 

*    Please show me minimal examples. 
*    What are two alternative approaches? 
*    What assumptions am I making? 

** Prompt **  : Please explain why AI is described as a multiplier of existing skills with concrete examples in web development. 

##   Configuring an AI chatbot for learning 

 If you want a    free AI chatbot to genuinely help you learn web development (instead of just spitting out code you don’t understand), you need to configure it in three ways: 

*    How you start each chat (your learning contract) 
*    How you ask questions (prompt patterns) 
*    How you verify and practice (so you don’t get tricked by confident nonsense) 

 Below is a setup that works well with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. 

###   Create a reusable learning contract message 

 At the start of a new chat, paste something    like the following learning contract and tweak it to your taste. 

 Learning contract (paste this at the top of the chat): 

```
You are my web dev tutor for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SQL, Python and Django. Teach me like a beginner who wants to become competent, not like someone who wants a quick copy-paste. Prefer short steps with checkpoints.
When giving code, also explain:
- what the code does
- why this approach is used
- common mistakes
Ask me 1–3 quick questions if needed (but do not stall). Always provide a tiny exercise after explaining a concept. 
When I paste an error, help me debug by:
- explaining likely causes
- telling me exactly what to check
- giving the minimal fix first
```

 If your chatbot supports  * custom instructions *  or  * memory *  , put the same content there so you don’t have to repeat it.   If it doesn’t, keep it in a note and paste it into each new chat. 

###   Pick a track so the bot teaches coherently 

 Free chatbots can be amazing, but they’ll happily jump around unless you set a structure.   Pick one learning track and stick with it for a few sessions: 

*    HTML semantics and structure 
*    CSS layout and styling 
*    JavaScript fundamentals 
*    SQL basics using SQLite 
*    Django basics 
*    Deployment concepts and scripting with Bash 

 Tell the chatbot: 

```
Use this track. If I ask something beyond the scope of my current track, briefly answer but then guide me back to the track.
```

###   Use prompt templates that force real learning 

 Prompt patterns    that make it more likely that the model will explain instead of    dumping code on you are shown in  * Table 1.3 *  : 

 
| ** Template ** || ** Example ** |
| --- | --- |
|  Explain, then quiz me  ||  Teach me  * \[topic\] *  like I’m new.   Use a simple example.   After each section, ask me a quick question to check understanding.   Don’t move on until I answer.  |
| --- | --- |
|  Socratic debugging  ||  I’m getting this error in  * \[language/framework\] *  .   Ask me the most important questions first, one at a time, and explain what each answer would imply.   Here’s the traceback:  * \[traceback\]. * |
|  Minimal code with “why”  ||  Show the smallest possible example of  * \[feature\] *  that handles  * \[functionality\] *  .   Explain each line.   Then give me one small change to implement.  |
|  Make me practice  ||  Give me a 20-minute exercise:  * \[task\] *  .   Provide requirements and hints only.   Don’t give the solution unless I ask.   For example, build a Django page that lists products from SQLite, with a search box using  ` GET `  parameters.  |
|  Compare options  ||  Explain three ways to structure a  * \[language/framework\] *  project using  * \[feature\] *  .   Give pros/cons and when to choose each.   For example, function views vs class views, apps layout.  |

 Table 1.3: Prompt templates for learning 

###   Make the bot work inside your actual project 

 You’ll get dramatically better help if you feed it the right context.   This will become easier once we use an AI tool integrated into your code editor or IDE, but you can also manually provide context even when using a separate AI chatbot. 

 Try to provide: 

*    Your goal (“I want a page that lists blog posts”) 
*    Your current code (the smallest relevant piece) 
*    The error message/traceback 
*    Your file names and where the code lives (  ` views.py `  ,  ` urls.py `  , template path) 

 This prevents the chatbot from guessing your setup. 

###   Put guardrails on code generation 

 Many readers skip this    step, but it makes a real difference. 

 Add these rules to your chat: 

```
You must follow these rules when your response includes code:
- Do not generate more than about 40 lines of code at once unless I ask.
- Prefer incremental changes with diffs.
- If you propose a change, show it as: what to delete, what to add.
- Tell me the one most likely issue first.
```

 This keeps the experience interactive and reduces the chance that you end up with a Frankenstein project. 

###   Use AI as a tutor, not a compiler 

 AI should not    be used as a tool that replaces your own implementation work.   A solid routine that should become a habit for you is to use the four-step learning loop, as shown in  * Figure 1.6 *  : 

1.   Ask for explanation + tiny example 
2.   Implement it yourself (even if it’s slow) 
3.   Paste your attempt and ask for feedback 
4.   Do a small variation (“Now add validation,” “Now add search,” and so on) 

![](Images/Image4168.png)

 Figure 1.6: The AI learning loop 

 Tell the chatbot explicitly: 

```
Don't write the final solution. Coach me through implementing it.
```

###   Verification habits 

 Chatbots (especially free ones) will be    wrong sometimes so you can encourage the AI to check themselves with the following prompts: 

*   ` List the assumptions you made about my project structure. `
*   ` What are 3 ways this could fail and how would I detect each? `
*   ` What's the simplest alternative approach? `

 If you want extra safety, cross-check tricky answers by asking a second chatbot the same question.   When they disagree, that’s your cue to test carefully. 

 You’ve now picked one or more AI chatbots as your learning coaches and seen how to get the best mentoring experience out of them.   Let’s now turn our attention to actively coding, rather than learning concepts. 

#   Coding with an AI assistant as your coworker 

 Although chatbots are great for learning, when building a complete web development project, you need a more specialized tool that works inside your code editor or IDE and can help with multi-step coding tasks (aka agentically, a horrible marketing word that I hope dates fast).   The goal of this section is to understand the pros and cons of various AI tools that integrate with your coding tools. 

** Good practice **  : If you follow only one setup for a code editor or IDE with an integrated coding assistant in this book, use VS Code with GitHub Copilot.   This combination is widely used, integrates cleanly with the workflows we will build, and provides the least friction for beginners. 

 Before we look at specific tools, there is an important factor to consider about their relationship to AI models. 

##   Understanding the tool–model relationship 

 When you start using AI coding    assistants, it is easy to think of each tool as a single, fixed system.   For example, you might assume that GitHub Copilot is one AI, in the same way that ChatGPT or Claude feels like a single product. 

 In reality, tools like Copilot are better understood as interfaces to multiple underlying models. 

 This means that when you use a tool like GitHub Copilot in a code editor or IDE like VS Code, you are not always talking to one specific AI system.   Instead, the tool can route your request to different models depending on the task, the feature you are using, or your subscription level. 

 AI tools are built in layers: 

*    The editor or interface (for example, VS Code with Copilot) 
*    The integration layer that connects your editor to AI services 
*    One or more underlying models that actually generate responses 

 In some cases, this includes models from different providers. 

 For example, inside Copilot you might: 

*    Get inline code completions from one model 
*    Use chat features powered by another model 
*    Select or be routed to models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 or Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 

 So even though you are using Copilot, the actual intelligence behind a response might come from a completely different system. 

 This affects how you choose tools: 

1.   First, tool choice and model choice are not the same thing.   You might prefer working in Copilot because it integrates with your editor, but still want to use a specific model like Claude Opus for certain tasks. 
2.   Second, results can vary even within the same tool.   If Copilot switches models or you change settings, you may see different styles of responses, levels of detail, or coding approaches. 
3.   Third, you can combine strengths.   For example:  
    *    Use Copilot for fast inline suggestions while coding 
    *    Use a Claude-powered chat for deeper explanations 
    *    Use a stronger model for complex debugging or design decisions 

 Do not think in terms of which single AI should I use.   Instead, think about: 

*    Which tool fits your workflow (for example, VS Code with Copilot)? 
*    Which model is best for the current task (for example, Claude Opus with high thinking level for reviewing the architecture of a complex project, or GPT-5 mini with fast thinking    for writing dozens of unit tests)? 

 As AI tools evolve, this separation will become more important.   The developers who get the most value are not the ones who pick a single tool and stick to it.   They are the ones who understand what is happening underneath and choose the right combination for the job. 

##   The importance of a great harness 

 A coding assistant or agent is composed of a model and a harness: 

*    The model is the raw intelligence 
*    The harness is everything that makes it usable 

 An  ** agent harness **  is    the software infrastructure surrounding a model that manages tool execution, memory, state persistence, and verification.   The harness is the complete software infrastructure wrapping a model, including the orchestration loop, tools, memory, context management, state persistence, error handling, and guardrails. 

 A  ** coding harness **  is the    software scaffold around a model that helps it write and edit code effectively.   Codex and Claude Code can be considered coding harnesses. 

 The harness provides six core capabilities: 

1.  ** Orchestration loop **  : The harness    turns one-shot responses into a loop: call model, take action, observe result, repeat. 
2.  ** Tool use **  : The harness connects the model to tools that provide access to the file system, terminal, tests, and APIs.   Without these tools, the model can only describe code.   With it, the system can change code. 
3.  ** Context management **  : A raw model has a limited context window.   The harness decides which files to include, how to summarize, and what to exclude.   . 
4.  ** Memory and state **  : LLMs are stateless by default.   The harness adds session memory and persistence across runs. 
5.  ** Execution environment **  : Codex and similar tools run in real environments that is part of the harness, like a sandbox, runtime, and execution logs. 
6.  ** Guardrails and control **  : The    harness enforces permissions and safety constraints. 

 A raw model is like a processor on its own, capable of computation but disconnected from everything else.   The harness is what surrounds it with memory, storage, and input/output, turning it into a complete system that can actually do useful work. 

 If you want the best coding assistant, you need to think about two aspects: 

*    Your model choice affects the balance of responsiveness with smarter reasoning 
*    Your harness is important to getting work done 

 The biggest improvements in coding assistants are coming from the harness, not the model.   To summarize, a harness is the system around an AI model that gives it tools, memory, and a workflow, turning it from a text generator into something that can complete real tasks. 

 Now let’s review some of the most popular coding assistants that can integrate with your preferred code editor or IDE (and model). 

##   GitHub Copilot 

 For hands-on learning, GitHub Copilot    is the option I would start with because it sits in your code editor or IDE (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, and so on) and suggests code completions, templates, and entire functions as you type. 

 GitHub Copilot is very different from the “Copilots” that are integrated into Windows, Office, and every other Microsoft product these days.   Please don’t be put off by its branding. 

 Copilot is best for learning by coding, not chatting.   Copilot doesn’t replace your preferred chatbot.   It reduces the need to repeatedly search for common code patterns.   It is widely used by developers because it works while you type and has access to your whole project context. 

 Strengths: 

*    Excellent    code autocomplete 
*    Works inside your code editor or IDE 
*    Uses your project context to improve suggestions 

 Weakness: 

*    Poor for    conceptual learning unless paired with a chatbot 

 Free vs paid plans for in: 

*   ** Free **  /  ** Student **  : Includes    up to 2,000 inline suggestions in IDEs per month and up to 50 premium requests per month, giving you a limited taste of Copilot’s capabilities.   Students get unlimited completions in IDEs and up to 300 premium requests per month. 
*   ** Paid **  : Copilot Pro (1,000 AI credits per month for $10 USD) / Pro+ (3,900 AI credits per month for $39 USD), unlocking more completions and integrations. 
*   ** Business **  /  ** Enterprise **  : $19 USD per user per month (with the option to purchase additional premium requests at $0.04 USD per request), $39 USD per user per month (GitHub Enterprise Cloud only). 

 You can learn about GitHub Copilot’s usage-based billing at the following link:  [  https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/billing/usage-based-billing-for-individuals  ](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/billing/usage-based-billing-for-individuals%20)

 Sign up for    GitHub Copilot at the following link:  [  https://github.com/features//copilot  ](https://github.com/features/)

 How to set it up for success: 

*    Install the Copilot plugin in your editor 
*    Start by coding the bare minimum and ask Copilot to suggest snippets like HTML layout, JavaScript functions, and REST views in Django 
*    When something is suggested, ask “why this pattern?”   in Copilot Chat.   That shifts you from being a copy-paste monkey to having a deeper understanding 

##   Google’s Gemini Code Assist 

 Google offers an AI    coding assistant that gives generous free assistance (many completions per month) and is integrated with major editors like VS Code.   It can be useful for prototyping HTML and JavaScript or debugging Django views because the bot understands the context of your changes and suggests larger blocks of code, not just individual lines. 

 Gemini Code Assist    is a tool that you may want to explore later, once you are comfortable with the basic concepts of using VS Code and GitHub Copilot. 

 Free vs Paid: 

*    Free: Individual    tier gives lots of completions monthly 
*    Paid/Standard: Adds deeper integrations and metrics 

 How to set it up for success: 

*    Install the Gemini Code Assist extension in your editor of choice 
*    Use natural language prompts while coding (“Create a responsive navbar in HTML + CSS + JavaScript”) 
*    For Django, work in the shell and ask for model definitions, migrations, and admin customizations interactively 

 You can sign up for    Gemini Code Assist at the following link:  [  https://codeassist.google/  ](https://codeassist.google/)

##   AI coding tool costs and capabilities 

 By the first half of 2026, AI coding    tools have become a normal part of many developer workflows, but their cost, limits, and reliability are still evolving. 

 In  * The Pragmatic Engineer *  ’s March 2026 survey, 95% of respondents said they use AI tools at least weekly, 55% said they regularly use AI agents, and Claude Code was both the most-used and most-loved tool in that survey. 

 Jellyfish’s latest engineering study says more than half of companies in its dataset use AI coding tools consistently, 64% generate a majority of their code with AI assistance, and higher-adoption teams are seeing about 2x the  ** pull request **  (  ** PR **  ) throughput    of low adopters. 

 You can read more about these studies and surveys at the following links:    https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/ai-tooling-2026 and https://jellyfish.co/newsroom/jellyfish-reveals-ais-real-impact-on-engineering-teams/  

 But that does not mean developers are serene about it.   The mood on Reddit, Hacker News, and other public channels is more like:  * this is unbelievably useful, slightly addictive, and constantly threatening to waste time or money if you use it badly *  . 

 Developers describe Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot as useful for end-to-end feature implementation, repo-wide refactors, planning, code review, and running multiple competing agents at once to compare outputs. 

 Reuters reported in    late March 2026 that Codex now has more than 2 million weekly active users, after a 3x increase in users and 5x increase in usage in the first quarter of 2026:  [  https://www.reuters.com/technology/openai-buy-python-toolmaker-astral-take-anthropic-2026-03-19/  ](https://www.reuters.com/technology/openai-buy-python-toolmaker-astral-take-anthropic-2026-03-19/%20)

###   Token and quota burn 

 A common    complaint is unclear cost and usage limits, especially token    burn and quota burn.   On  ` r/codex `  , multiple March 2026 posts complain that weekly usage disappears much faster than expected, with people reporting things like  * takes 10% of my weekly limit per task *  ,  * 75% of my weekly limit from like 3 days of using it *  , and screenshots showing almost exhausted limits after only a couple of days of normal work.   Other posts say token burn suddenly spiked in mid-March without an obvious change in process. 

 GitHub Copilot users are complaining about the same thing in a different form.   Since Copilot mixes unlimited completions with capped premium requests, the argument is less about raw tokens and more about which models chew through premium allowance too quickly.   In March 2026 discussions, users complained that Claude Opus inside Copilot was consuming premium requests much faster than expected, and others reported higher token usage after recent updates. 

** Prompt **  : Please explain token usage in simple terms with a real example of a coding session.   What causes high token usage in AI coding tools and how can I reduce it? 

###   A practical approach to token usage 

 A practical approach is to use    tiering instead of picking the “smartest” model and using it for everything.   Use a cheaper or capped tool for broad exploration, boilerplate, and repetitive edits.   Escalate to the expensive frontier model only for architecture, tricky debugging, or large refactors. 

 You can see that pattern directly in public discussion.   One Reddit user says they  * plan with Claude initially and review with Codex *  , others recommend sticking to Sonnet or Haiku for normal work and saving Opus    for tougher tasks, and Copilot users talk about using cheaper models for iterative back-and-forth because premium models burn quota too fast. 

** Good practice **  : Use a cheap model to search, summarize, lint, scaffold, and rewrite.   Use a premium model for hard reasoning.   Use a separate reviewer model to check the work of your primary model.   The developers getting wrecked on cost are often the ones running frontier models on  ` xhigh `  thinking levels for tasks that should have been handled by a cheaper pass first. 

** Prompt **  : Please design a low-cost workflow using free and paid AI tools for a beginner. 

###   Pricing and choosing between plans 

 What the public chatter    suggests is this rough pattern: newbies and students are mostly using free tiers and educational entitlements; working individual developers go for the $10 to $20 range plans; and the $100 to $200 plans are mainly justified by heavy users who are doing hours of daily agentic coding and believe they are getting far more than the list price back in value. 

 You can read a typical discussion about the best value-for-money combination of AI subscriptions at the following link:  [  https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeCode/comments/1rp294g/the\_best\_value\_for\_money\_combination\_of\_ai/  ](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeCode/comments/1rp294g/the_best_value_for_money_combination_of_ai/)

###   Comparing developers’ opinions about AI tools 

 Anthropic’s Claude    Code is praised as the strongest pure coding agent    experience by a lot of power users, especially in smaller teams, and  * The Pragmatic Engineer *  ’s survey that I linked to earlier says it is currently the most loved tool. 

 OpenAI’s Codex    is praised for feeling more direct and engineering-oriented, but  ` r/codex `  in April 2026 was full of anxiety about unpredictable quota burn.   OpenAI’s own positioning is that Codex is included inside paid ChatGPT tiers, which makes it appealing to people who already live in that ecosystem. 

 GitHub Copilot    is still the safe default choice of coding assistant.   It is cheaper than most paid competitors for individuals, deeply integrated into mainstream IDEs, and much more natural for enterprise procurement.  * The Pragmatic Engineer *  survey says larger enterprises still skew toward Copilot, so if you work for a corporation, it is the most likely tool that you will be expected to use.   But the knock against it is that it no longer feels as cutting-edge or as loved by power users as    Claude Code. 

** Good practice: **  If a vendor changes limits, prices, or defaults in a way users hate, developers often switch tools quickly.   So, in many ways, it doesn’t matter much for beginners which one you pick to get started because you might switch between providers many times in a few months!   So, pick a plan that you can pay for month-to-month and cancel at will. 

###   Mixing models and prompting styles 

 Some    developers use multiple models against the same task, use one model for planning and another for implementation, or keep a cheap general assistant plus one premium coding specialist.   Effective use depends on knowing when to stop, when to simplify by trimming context, or when to switch tools, not on the person using the best-benchmarked model. 

 Some developers also adjust how they prompt and interact with models, even to the point of applying psychology that is usually only applied to fellow humans, as in the following link:  [  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47357042  ](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47357042%20)

 I recommend you start with one simple, low-cost tool, and one premium specialist, not five subscriptions.   Copilot Free or Pro is the entry point combined with ChatGPT Plus with Codex or Claude Pro.   The $200 plans only make sense once you are clearly running into limits every week and can point to actual throughput gains.   Higher-cost plans are usually only worthwhile for heavy daily use, but a beginner who jumps straight there is usually paying tuition for confusion. 

##   AI agents and multi-agent workflows 

 You have already seen how AI assistants can help you write code, explain concepts, and guide your learning.   AI agents    build on that idea, but the difference is that an AI agent is not responding to a single prompt.   It    is trying to complete a task over multiple steps, and the agent is taking more initiative.   Instead of waiting for your next prompt, it may: 

*    Break a task into smaller steps 
*    Modify multiple files 
*    Run commands or tests 
*    Revise its approach based on what happens 

 Where things become even more interesting is when multiple agents are involved. 

 Some tools use a coordinating agent that manages a group of smaller, specialized agents.   Each of these subagents focuses on a specific type of work. 

 For example, a system might include: 

*    A planning agent that decides what needs to be done 
*    A coding agent that writes or edits code 
*    A testing agent that runs tests and reports failures 
*    A review agent that checks for mistakes or improvements 

 The coordinating agent    assigns tasks to these subagents, collects their results, and decides what to do next.   This creates a routine that is closer to a small team than a single assistant. 

 This approach    can be very effective.   Different agents can focus on what they do best, and the system can iterate more quickly across multiple steps.   The agents often have different capabilities or thinking levels, or may even be from different companies.   For example, some advanced developers have found that OpenAI’s Codex at very high thinking level is best for planning, and then they hand off the implementation to Claude Code Sonnet, or a local model like Qwen3-Coder-Next or DeepSeek Coder.   In  [* Chapter 11 *](#11.xhtml#_idTextAnchor764)  ,  * Setting Up Your Project Environment *  , I cover local models in more detail. 

###   Why agents matter 

 At first glance, multi-agent systems sound like a clear upgrade.   In many cases, they are.   They can handle larger, more complex tasks, work across multiple files and layers of a project, and catch issues earlier through built-in review or testing steps. 

 But there is a cost that is easy to overlook. 

 Every time an agent performs a step, it sends and receives data.   In a multi-agent system, this happens multiple times per task, and often between several agents.   This has a direct impact on token usage.   If multiple agents are communicating with each other, the same context may be passed around several times.   This can increase token usage quickly, even for tasks that seem small. 

 This is why developers often notice that agent-based tools feel more expensive or burn through quota faster than simple chat-based tools. 

 For learning, it is important to use these tools with some discipline. 

 If you rely on a multi-agent system to build large features from scratch, it may produce working code, but you risk paying for a lot of computation that does not actually help you learn. 

 A better approach is to: 

*    Use smaller, focused tasks rather than large open-ended goals 
*    Limit how much the agent is allowed to do in one go 
*    Review each step instead of accepting everything automatically 
*    Be aware that more automation usually means higher token usage 

 As you gain experience, you can start to take advantage of multi-agent workflows for more complex tasks.   At that point, the trade-offs between speed, cost, and understanding will become clearer. 

 We will look at AI agents in more detail in the third part of this book when we build a real-world project.   For now, let’s review some practical tips for working with AI. 

** Prompt **  : When should I switch from chatbot to IDE-integrated assistant? 

##   Practical tips for collaborating with any AI 

 Here’s how to make these tools    actual teachers instead of glorified code generators. 

*   ** State your learning goal up front **  : Instead of “write me a Django view”, ask “teach me how Django views handle GET vs POST with examples.”   That forces the AI to explain, not just produce an end result. 
*   ** Ask for step-by-step explanations **  : Always include phrasing like “explain line by line and why it matters.” 
*   ** Iterate with small prompts **  :    Instead of huge requests, break things down into smaller steps.   You can always use follow-ups like “now expand on this” when you want to go deeper. 
*   ** Use editor integration for practice **  : Chatbots inside editors like Copilot, Gemini, and DeepSeek make learning contextual from the active project and its code files.   You’re not just learning abstract theory, the chatbot is applying it to your current code. 
*   ** Validate with multiple sources. **  For tricky concepts, ask two assistants (for example, ChatGPT and Claude) and compare answers.   Discrepancies often reveal subtle nuances    you’d miss otherwise. 

 A useful prompt is the following: 

```
Act as a strategic advisor. Based on my goal below, recommend ONE best option and explain why it is superior to alternatives. Then, list two backup options and specify exactly when I should choose them instead. My goal is [Insert your goal here]
```

 Anthropic has useful prompt guidance on their website that also applies to most models, found at the following link:  [  https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices  ](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices%20)

 Now let’s review some key information about using AI tools and how AI has changed the role of software developers. 

#   Pros and cons of AI tools 

 Many people claim that human developers will soon be obsolete because AI will write software autonomously and make coders unnecessary.   But I am unconvinced that we have entered anything resembling a post-developer world. 

##   Companies are increasingly using AI tools 

 It is true that companies are    increasingly adopting AI tools.   For example, an article in Forbes reported that AI writes over 25% of the code committed at Google.   But human developers remain deeply involved in the process, guiding AI, reviewing its output, editing the code, and shaping it into a coherent product.   AI is a tool controlled by humans, not a replacement for humans. 

##   Human + AI = success 

 While AI tools like    GitHub Copilot can produce impressive results in well-defined tasks, they still require a human hand on the tiller.   To mix my metaphors, using AI in development is like flying a plane with cruise control: the aircraft goes where you point it, but without constant guidance and corrections from a skilled pilot, it could drift off course, and critical steps in the flight like landing and takeoff should be done entirely under human control. 

 As a software developer using    AI tools, if you do not understand the code being generated, you won’t know when or how to correct it.   This limitation is central to why the idea that we are entering a post-human programmer world is exaggerated. 

##   Limits of AI 

 There are plenty of    tasks where current large language models struggle.   Some of the most hyped tools have failed in real testing contexts.   You might find that your AI tool can only complete a subset of assignments satisfactorily and you ultimately spend more time working around its mistakes than you would have writing the code yourself. 

 These results suggest that AI in its current form is good at well-scoped, repetitive tasks, but poor at open-ended or complex development problems without significant human intervention. 

 There has also been interesting recent research suggesting a gap between perceived and actual productivity gains from AI assistance.   A 2025 randomized controlled trial by the nonprofit research group  ** METR **  (  ** Model Evaluation & Threat Research **  ) reported that developers using AI tools actually took longer to complete tasks compared to those who did not use AI, even while they felt like they    were faster.   This speaks to the psychological allure of AI promises versus the messy reality of real engineering work. 

 Researchers found developers spent extra time prompting the AI, reviewing suggestions, correcting errors, and integrating generated code. 

 In other words: less typing, more verification.   Developers had to verify and correct AI suggestions that were often only broadly accurate. 

 The key paper is  * Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity *  by researchers at METR.   The main finding was that developers using AI tools took 19% longer to complete tasks than those who did not.   Yet they believed AI made them faster by about 20–24%.   You can read more at the following link:  [  https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/  ](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)

 This study does  * not *  mean AI always slows developers down.   It applies mainly to experienced developers with familiar codebases and complex real-world tasks. 

 Other studies show the opposite. 

 For example, GitHub Copilot users completed tasks 55.8% faster in controlled experiments.   You can read  * The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot *  paper at the following link:  [  https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590  ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590%20)

 Google engineers were about 21% faster in an enterprise trial that you can read about at the following    link:  [  https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944  ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944%20)

 So the reality of AI-enhanced coding in the current era is messy. 

##   How AI impacts junior and senior developers differently 

 This is one of the most    revealing things about AI and software development.   It looks paradoxical at first, but it actually makes perfect sense once you unpack how juniors and seniors think. 

 The core idea in one sentence is that AI tends to be most helpful for junior developers because it reduces the friction of writing code and helps close common knowledge gaps.   For senior developers, however, the benefits can be less consistent, since AI can sometimes interrupt deeper, expert-level thinking. 

 Junior developers often struggle with things like syntax, boilerplate, unfamiliar APIs and libraries, patterns they have not encountered yet, and even the basic question of what code to write in the first place.   Their cognitive load is often highest at the mechanical level, and AI works well as a powerful autocomplete tool and an on-demand tutor.   As a result, using AI to learn and write code can lead to major productivity gains. 

 Senior developers, on the other hand, typically spend more mental effort on higher-level concerns such as architecture decisions, trade-offs, system constraints, legacy code behavior, performance, scalability, security, and subtle bugs.   Their cognitive load is more conceptual than mechanical, and they usually already know how to write code quickly. 

 In these cases, AI may fill fewer gaps.   It can also introduce noise, generic advice, or context-missing suggestions that appear plausible but do not hold up in a specific system.   This can increase review time, create distractions, and in some situations slow progress rather than speeding it up. 

** Prompt **  : Please explain why AI helps junior developers more than senior developers.   And what skills should a junior developer focus on to become a senior-level thinker early? 

##   AI shifts work from writing code to judging code 

 Historically, junior    developers spent more time learning how to write code, while senior developers spent more time deciding what code should exist in the first place.   AI is pushing more of the profession in that direction.   Writing code is becoming less important as a standalone skill.   Understanding systems, architecture, trade-offs, and behavior is becoming more important. 

 In practical terms, the value of a developer is shifting away from typing code and toward thinking clearly about what should be built, how it should behave, and how to recognize when an AI-generated solution is wrong, brittle, insecure, or simply a bad fit. 

 That is one of the main reasons this book is structured the way it is.   Before you build the larger project later in the book, you first spend time learning the individual languages, frameworks, tools, and concepts.   This book is not trying to turn you into a human syntax machine.   It is trying to help you build the judgment needed to direct AI well, review its work intelligently, and make sound engineering decisions. 

 This is why, although AI can accelerate your learning experience for web development, ultimately you do still need to learn HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SQL, Python, and so on, so that you can then apply your human judgment to the code your AI assistant writes for you when building a complete project. 

##   Developer job market 

 Even factual sources of evidence    like the job market, where the idea that AI is the main cause of employment challenges for developers is prevalent, can be misleading.   While layoffs and hiring slowdowns are real, they are likely caused by broader macroeconomic factors, such as high interest rates and investment contractions, rather than a sudden lack of need for human developers.   Some companies may hold back hiring because of myths about imminent AI takeover, but I believe this narrative is hurting growth more than actual automation is. 

 Two things have remained true since ChatGPT burst into society’s consciousness in November 2023: companies still need human developers, and AI evangelists continue to claim that developers will be obsolete any week now. 

 Neither of these points seems likely to change soon.   Once companies fully recognize that AI functions best as an enhancer of human capability and not a replacement, they will resume more vigorous hiring.   Rather than fearing the machines, aspiring developers should see this era as one where skilled developers using AI well can get more done than developers who ignore it or trust it blindly. 

##   It’s all about you 

 I’ll end this discussion with a cautionary note for you, my reader.   How learners and early-career developers like you integrate AI into your education and eventually into your daily development lives is important.   If you rely too heavily on AI’s output without understanding it, you risk building brittle knowledge that fails when AI inevitably stumbles. 

 Conversely, when used as a tutor or assistant that helps explain errors, clarify concepts, and guide exploration, AI can be a useful learning aid.   I wrote this book to help you use these new AI tools to help you learn faster, but you still do need to work hard at it. 

** Warning! **

 AI decreases critical thinking capability through a process called cognitive offloading.   It is fine to rely on an AI for relatively simple tasks but don’t allow AI to take over your judgment. 

** Prompt **  : What is cognitive offloading in learning, and how does it apply to AI coding assistants? 

 No one knows how AI models will evolve, and the world still needs people who understand how to build software.   Rather than getting discouraged by hype or fear, I recommend that you use AI, but do not outsource your judgment to it.   The world still needs people who understand how software works because AI tools still do not really have that understanding. 

#   Practice, references, and resources 

 In this section, you will be tested on what you’ve learned in this chapter and provided with useful links to reference materials and resources. 

##   Studying with NotebookLM 

 Google’s  ** NotebookLM **  is a useful    tool for learning because it grounds AI responses in sources that you control.   Instead of asking general questions and getting answers based on a model’s broad training, you upload your own material such as book chapters, documentation, or notes, and the AI works only within that context.   This makes NotebookLM particularly effective for studying, since you can treat it as a focused tutor for a specific topic. 

 A practical routine is to upload a chapter or set of notes, then ask questions like  * summarize this section *  ,  * explain this concept in simpler terms *  , or  * quiz me on the key ideas *  . 

 You can also ask it to compare sections, generate examples, or identify gaps in your understanding.   Because every response is tied back to your source material, it reduces the risk of irrelevant or incorrect explanations and helps reinforce what you are actually trying to learn, rather than sending you off into unrelated topics.

#   HTML – Structuring Your Web Pages 

 This chapter covers the basics    of  ** HTML **  (  ** HyperText Markup Language **  ).   You’ll learn the key concepts about HTML and then use the AI to generate a simple page, and in doing so, learn about elements, tags, and attributes. 

 By the end of this chapter, you will be able to read, write, and understand HTML as a structured description of a web page, and confidently build simple, meaningful pages that form a solid foundation for everything that comes next. 

 In this chapter, we will cover the following topics: 

*    What is HTML? 
*    Building a basic web page 
*    Working with forms and inputs 
*    AI exercises 
*    Other markup languages  
    
     Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link:  [  https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch02-html/readme.md  ](https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch02-html/readme.md%20)
    

#   What is HTML? 

 HTML    stands for HyperText Markup Language.   That sounds scary, but the idea is simple. 

 HTML is not a programming language: 

*    It does not make decisions 
*    It does not run logic 
*    It does not calculate anything 

 HTML    describes the structure and meaning of content on a web page. 

 HTML is the page’s structure.   It defines: 

*    What text is a heading 
*    What text is a paragraph 
*    What counts as a list 
*    Where do links point? 
*    Which images belong on the page? 
*    How tabular data is organized 

 CSS makes things look good.   You will learn about CSS in  [* Chapter 3 *](#03.xhtml#_idTextAnchor154) * , CSS – Styling Your Web Pages *  .   For this chapter, ignore how things look and focus on what they are and how they are structured. 

 JavaScript makes things interactive.   The web pages that you create in this chapter will be static.   In  [* Chapter 5 *](#05.xhtml#_idTextAnchor266) * , JavaScript – Making Web Pages Interactive *  , you will write JavaScript code to make them come alive. 

 HTML decides what things are.   Without HTML, the web would just be a stream of unstructured text. 

##   HTML is made of elements 

 HTML is    built from  ** tags **  to form  ** elements **  .   A tag is the actual markup syntax enclosed in angle brackets, such    as  ` <p> `  or  ` </p> `  , which    tells the browser    how to interpret content.   An element, on the other hand, is the complete structure that includes the opening tag, the content, and the closing tag. 

 For example,  ` <p>Hello</p> `  is a paragraph element, made up of the opening  ` <p> `  tag, the text  ` Hello `  , and the closing  ` </p> `  tag.   Tags are the building blocks, while elements are the full constructs created from those tags. 

 Most elements look like this: 

```
<p>This is a paragraph.</p>
```

*   ` <p> `  means  * start a new paragraph *
*   ` </p> `  means  * end of the paragraph *
*    Everything in between is the content of the paragraph 

 In HTML,  ** attributes **  provide    additional information about an element and are placed inside the    opening tag.   They usually come in name–value pairs, such as  ` class="intro" `  or  ` href="https://example.com" `  , and they modify how the element behaves or is displayed. 

 For example, in  ` <a href="https://example.com">Visit</a> `  , the  ` href `  attribute tells the browser where the link should go.   While the element defines the structure and meaning, attributes refine or configure that element’s behavior. 

 Two attributes appear constantly in HTML:  ` id `  and  ` class `  .   An  ` id `  identifies one unique element on a page.   A  ` class `  labels one or more elements as belonging to the same group.   Later, CSS and JavaScript will use these heavily.   For now, the important  ` id `  idea is simple:  ` id `  is for one specific element, while  ` class `  can be shared. 

 Some elements    are  ** void elements **  , like  ` <img> `  or  ` <br> `  , which do not have closing tags or inner content.   Others    are  ** container elements **  , such as  ` <div> `  or  ` <section> `  , which wrap content and can include other elements inside them. 

 A  ` <div> `  is a generic    container element with no inherent meaning.   It’s useful for grouping content for styling, but it should not replace semantic elements like  ` <section> `  ,  ` <nav> `  , or  ` <p> `  when those are more appropriate. 

 It is also important to know that elements can be nested, meaning one element can sit inside another to create a hierarchy.   Proper nesting is important because incorrect structure can lead to unexpected rendering or accessibility issues. 

** Good practice **  : Accessibility in web development means designing and structuring content so that it can be used by everyone, including people with disabilities such as visual, hearing, motor, or cognitive impairments.   This includes using proper HTML structure, meaningful text alternatives like  ` alt `  attributes for images, and clear navigation so assistive technologies such as screen readers can interpret the page correctly. 

 Another key idea is the distinction    between  ** block-level elements **  and  ** inline elements **  .   Block-level elements, like  ` <p> `  and  ` <h1> `  , typically start on a new line and take up the full width    available, while inline elements, like  ` <span> `  or  ` <a> `  , flow within text without breaking the layout. 

 Modern HTML emphasizes semantic elements, such as  ` <article> `  ,  ` <nav> `  , and  ` <footer> `  , which describe the meaning of content rather than just its appearance.   Using these correctly improves accessibility, search    engine understanding, and overall code clarity. 

 You will reuse these ideas throughout the chapter. 

** Prompt **  : Please explain the difference between semantic HTML and non-semantic HTML with real-world examples and why it matters for accessibility. 

##   Comments in HTML 

 HTML comments    let you    leave notes in the source code that are not shown on the page.   They look like this: 

```
<!-- This is a comment -->
```

 Comments are useful for reminders, temporary notes, or explaining examples in teaching code.   They are not a way to hide sensitive information, because anyone can still view the page source. 

##   The basic structure of a web page 

 Every HTML page    follows the same    overall pattern: 

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My first page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello world</h1>
    <p>This is my first web page.</p>
  </body>
</html>
```

 Each part has a distinct role: 

*   ` <!DOCTYPE html> `  tells the browser  * this is modern HTML *  , meaning standards-based HTML, specifically HTML5.   If you omit it, browsers may fall back to  ** quirks mode **  , which emulates legacy behavior from the early web to maintain    compatibility with very old pages.   That can lead to inconsistent layout, especially with CSS. 
*   ` <html> `  wraps the entire document. 
*   ` <head> `  contains metadata like the title, character encoding, and links to CSS for applying styles. 
*   ` <body> `  contains everything the user can see. 

 Nothing visible on    the page goes outside  ` <body> `  .   The page title is defined in  ` <head> `  and usually appears in the browser tab. 

** Prompt **  : Please show me examples of good and bad HTML structure and explain what makes one better than the other.

** Prompt **  : Please show me the HTML for a basic web page with examples of headings, paragraphs, and lists, so that I can learn about how web pages are structured, with an explanation of all the elements. 

##   Headings give content hierarchy 

 Headings    define document structure.   Their visual size is a styling decision.   The    font family and font size for each heading level will be applied using CSS later and do not have to match the level number! 

 HTML has six heading levels: 

```
<h1>Main page title</h1>
<h2>Section title</h2>
<h3>Subsection title</h3>
<h4>Sub-subsection title</h4>
<h5>Sub-sub-subsection title</h5>
<h6>Sub-sub-sub-subsection title</h6>
```

 Key beginner rule: 

*   ` <h1> `  is the most important heading on the page 
*   ` <h2> `  is a section inside that page 
*   ` <h3> `  is a subsection inside an  ` <h2> `

 Treat headings as part of the page outline, not as a way to pick a bigger font. 

 Search engines, screen readers, and accessibility tools rely heavily on correct heading structure.   Using    headings purely for visual effect is one    of the most common beginner mistakes. 

##   Paragraphs hold readable text 

 Normal    text belongs in    paragraphs: 

```
<p>This is a paragraph of text.</p>
```

 Browsers automatically add spacing between paragraphs. 

 You do not press  * Enter *  repeatedly like in Word.   In fact, extra whitespace characters like carriage returns, tabs, and spaces are ignored when rendering HTML in a browser! 

 HTML is about meaning, not layout. 

##   Links connect the web 

 Links are    what connect    pages into the web: 

```
<a href="https://example.com">Visit Example Website</a>
```

` Here: `

*   ` <a> `  stands for  * anchor *
*   ` href `  is the destination 
*    The text between the tags is what users click on 

 Links can point to: 

*    Other websites 
*    Other pages on the same site 
*    Sections within the same page 

 Without links, HTML pages are just isolated documents. 

##   Images add visual content 

 Images    are embedded    using the  ` <img> `  element: 

```
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo of a cat">
```

 Note the following about the preceding code: 

*   ` <img> `  has no closing tag 
*   ` src `  is the image file location 
*   ` alt `  describes the image in words  
    
    ` <img> `  is a void element, which means it has no closing tag because it doesn’t wrap any other content or contain nested elements.   Other void elements you’ll encounter include  ` <br> `  (line break),  ` <hr> `  (horizontal rule), and  ` <input> `  for forms.   While  ` <img> `  does not need a closing tag, it does need certain attributes to be considered well-formed and accessible, like  ` src `  and  ` alt `  . 
    

 The  ` alt `  text    is important because it carries meaning when the image cannot.   Screen readers rely    on it.   Search engines read it.   If the image fails to load, the text still communicates meaning. 

 HTML treats images as content, not decoration.   Decorative images, such as using emojis as custom bullets in lists, are usually handled in CSS. 

** Prompt **  : Please show me how to write accessible HTML for images, links, and forms. 

##   Lists group related items 

 HTML    supports two main list    types. 

** Unordered lists **  use    the  ` <ul> `  tag: 

```
<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>
```

 This means a list in which order does not matter. 

** Ordered lists **  use    the  ` <ol> `  tag: 

```
<ol>
  <li>Preheat the oven</li>
  <li>Mix ingredients</li>
  <li>Bake for 30 minutes</li>
</ol>
```

 This means  * steps in a specific sequence *  . 

 Each  ** list item **  lives inside  ` <li> `  . 

##   Tables structure data, not layout 

 Tables    are for data, not    page layout: 

```
<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Age</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Alex</td>
    <td>32</td>
  </tr>
</table>
```

 Conceptually: 

*   ` <table> `  wraps the data 
*   ` <tr> `  is a  ** table row **
*   ` <th> `  is a  ** table header **  cell 
*   ` <td> `  is a  ** table data **  cell 

 Tables are best when showing: 

*    Prices 
*    Schedules 
*    Statistics 
*    Comparisons 

 Using tables to position content for layout is an outdated practice and causes accessibility problems. 

##   HTML elements nest inside one another 

 HTML    elements form    a tree structure. 

 Example: 

```
<body>
  <section>
    <h2>About me</h2>
    <p>I write books.</p>
  </section>
</body>
```

 Here: 

*   ` <section> `  lives inside  ` <body> `
*   ` <h2> `  and  ` <p> `  live inside  ` <section> `

 This    nesting is how browsers understand relationships    between content. 

** Prompt **  : Please give me examples of incorrectly nested HTML and explain why they break things. 

##   Using <div> as a generic container 

 Sometimes you need to    group several pieces of content together without adding any specific meaning.   That is what the  ` <div> `  element is for. 

 A  ` <div> `  is a generic block-level container.   It does not tell the browser or a screen reader what the content means.   It simply groups content together. 

 For example: 

```
<div>
  <h2>About this book</h2>
  <p>This book teaches web development with AI as a learning partner.</p>
</div>
```

 This can be useful when you want to style or script a group of elements later with CSS or JavaScript. 

 But  ` <div> `  should not be your first choice when a semantic element fits better.   If the content is a section of the page, use  ` <section> `  .   If it is navigation, use  ` <nav> `  .   If it is a paragraph, use  ` <p> `  .   If it is the page footer, use  ` <footer> `  . 

 A good beginner rule is this: use  ` <div> `  when you need a container, not when you need meaning.   A page full of  ` <div> `  elements can still work, but it tells humans and tools much less about the structure of the content.   Semantic elements make your HTML easier to read, easier to maintain, and more accessible. 

** Prompt **  : Please show me three examples where  ` <div> `  is appropriate and three where a semantic element would be better. 

##   HTML describes meaning, not appearance 

 For beginners, this distinction makes the rest of the web technology stack easier to understand. 

 HTML answers questions like: 

*    Is this a heading? 
*    Is this a paragraph? 
*    Is this navigation? 
*    Is this a list of items? 
*    Is this tabular data? 

 HTML does not answer: 

*    Should this be blue? 
*    Should this be centered? 
*    Should this animate? 

 That separation is deliberate.   It keeps the web flexible, accessible, and device-independent. 

** Good practice **  : Do not try to memorize every HTML tag.   Start by asking what each piece of content is.   Is it the main heading?   A paragraph?   A navigation link?   A list of steps?   A table of data?   Once you can answer those questions, the tags become easier to choose, and AI-generated HTML becomes easier to review. 

** Prompt **  : What are ARIA attributes and when should beginners care about them? 

##   What good structure gives you 

 When HTML is written properly: 

*    Browsers can display it correctly on any screen size 
*    Search engines understand the content 
*    Screen readers can navigate the page 
*    CSS and JavaScript become easier to apply later 

 A page can look fine in a browser while still having poor structure or accessibility. 

 Well-structured HTML is easier to maintain.   Bad HTML creates maintenance problems almost immediately. 

** Prompt **  : How do search engines use HTML structure to understand a page? 

##   HTML DOM (document object model) 

 The HTML  ** DOM **  (  ** Document Object Model **  ) is how    the browser represents an HTML page internally after it has been loaded.   Instead of thinking of your page as plain text, the browser turns it into a tree of objects that it can understand, manipulate, and render. 

 Let’s see how it works with a simple HTML example: 

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p>This is a paragraph.</p>
  </body>
</html>
```

 When the browser reads the preceding code, it does not keep it as raw text.   It parses the HTML and builds a tree structure, where each element becomes a node: 

```
Document
 └── html
      ├── head
      │    └── title
      │         └── "My Page"
      └── body
           ├── h1
           │    └── "Hello"
           └── p
                └── "This is a paragraph."
```

 Here is how to think about this: 

*   ` Document `  is the root of everything 
*    Each HTML element becomes a node in the tree 
*    Elements can have child nodes (like  ` <body> `  containing  ` <h1> `  and  ` <p> `  ) 
*    Text inside elements also becomes nodes 

 This structure reflects the nesting you write in HTML.   If you nest elements incorrectly, the DOM will also be incorrect, which can lead to confusing behavior. 

 What the browser actually does (step by step): 

1.   It downloads the HTML file 
2.   It reads it from top to bottom 
3.   It parses each tag and creates nodes 
4.   It builds the DOM tree in memory 
5.   It uses that tree to render the page 

 The DOM    is not just for display.   CSS uses the DOM to decide what to style, and JavaScript uses the DOM to read and change the page dynamically after the page is initially rendered.   For example, JavaScript can do things like: 

*    Change text inside  ` <h1> `
*    Add new elements 
*    Remove elements 
*    Respond to user actions 

 HTML is the source document.   The DOM is the browser’s live tree built from that document.   Once the page is loaded, the browser works with the DOM, not your original HTML file.   The DOM is the browser’s internal representation of your HTML as a tree of objects.   If your HTML structure is clean and logical, the DOM will be easy to work with.   This is why logical thinking about structure matters more than raw typing speed. 

##   The beginner takeaway 

 If you remember only one thing from this chapter, it should be this: 

 HTML is about what content is, not how it looks. 

 Once you understand that distinction, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript make more sense as separate tools. 

** Prompt **  : Please show me 10 common beginner HTML mistakes and how to fix them.
