#   Building a basic web page 

 In this section, you’re going to make a tiny  * about me *  page, then watch it update instantly as you edit it. 

##   Build a web page in VS code and preview it live 

 Create a    project    folder: 

1.   Make a new folder on your computer called  ` about-me-webpage `
2.   Inside it, create another folder called  ` images `

 Your folder structure will look like this: 

```
about-me-webpage/
  images/
```

 Open the  ` about-me-webpage `  folder in VS Code: 

1.   Open VS Code. 
2.   Go to  ** File **  | Open Folder... 
3.   Choose  ` about-me-webpage. ` 
    
     Opening the folder (not just a single file) is important because live preview tools behave better when VS Code knows what your project root is. 
    

1.   If you    see a warning about trusting the authors    of files in this folder, check the box and click the  ** Yes, I trust the authors **  button, as shown in  * Figure 2.4 *  : 

![](Images/B34553_02_04.png)

 Figure 2.4: Trusting the authors of files in this folder in VS Code 

1.   In VS Code Explorer (left side), click  ** New File **  , and name it  ` index.html `  , as shown in  * Figure 2.5 *  : 

![](Images/B34553_02_05.png)

 Figure 2.5: VS Code Explorer and its New File button 

1.   Add the    following HTML to the empty file (this example includes everything you’ve learned with important elements highlighted).   Paste    this into  ` index.html `  : 

 This HTML file is available from the following link:  [  https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/index.html  ](https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/index.html)

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" 
          content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Mark's First Web Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Mark's First Web Page</h1>
    <p>
      Welcome! This page is a simple example of HTML structure: headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, and a table.
    </p>
    <h2>About this page</h2>
    <p>
      HTML tells the browser what each piece of content <em>is</em>.
      Styling comes later (that's CSS), and interactivity comes later (that's JavaScript).
    </p>
    <h2>Useful link</h2>
    <p>
      Here's a link to learn more about HTML:
      <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML">MDN Web Docs: HTML</a>.
    </p>
    <h2>Image</h2>
    <p>
      Below is an image. You can use a web image URL, or a local image file.
      The <strong>alt</strong> text describes the image for screen readers and when the image can't load.
    </p>
    <!-- Option A: Use a local image -->
    <!-- Save an image as images/profile.jpg and use this: -->
    <!-- <img src="images/profile.jpg" alt="A friendly profile photo"> -->
    <!-- Option B: Use a placeholder image from the web -->
    <img
      src="https://via.placeholder.com/640x240.png?text=My+First+Image"
      alt="A placeholder banner that says My First Image"
    >
    <h2>Lists</h2>
    <p>Unordered list (a list where the order doesn't matter):</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Headings organize the page</li>
      <li>Paragraphs hold normal text</li>
      <li>Links connect pages together</li>
    </ul>
    <p>Ordered list (a list of steps):</p>
    <ol>
      <li>Create a folder for your project</li>
      <li>Add an <code>index.html</code> file</li>
      <li>Open it with Live Preview</li>
    </ol>
    <h2>Table</h2>
    <p>
      Tables are for data. Here's a tiny "learning plan" table:
    </p>
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th>Topic</th>
          <th>What you'll practice</th>
          <th>Time (minutes)</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr>
          <td>Headings</td>
          <td>Page outline and sections</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <td>Links</td>
          <td>Link to another page</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <td>Images</td>
          <td>Add alt text</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <h2>Next idea</h2>
    <p>
      Try editing the text above and watch the preview update instantly.
      When you're ready, you can add CSS to make it look nicer.
    </p>
  </body>
</html>
```

 Note the    following about    the preceding code: 

*    Document structure:  ` <!DOCTYPE html> `  ,  ` <html> `  ,  ` <head> `  ,  ` <title> `  ,  ` <body> `
*    Headings:  ` <h1> `  ,  ` <h2> `
*    Paragraphs:  ` <p> `
*    Links:  ` <a href="..."> `
*    Images:  ` <img src="..." alt="..."> `

 If you see a broken image icon instead of the picture, it may be because the external image service is temporarily unavailable.   Your HTML is still correct.   Try switching to Option A which uses a local image file by saving any image to the correct path and filename  ` images/profile.jpg `  and uncomment the local  ` <img> `  element. 

*    Lists:  ` <ul> `  +  ` <li> `  , and  ` <ol> `  +  ` <li> `
*    Tables:  ` <table> `  ,  ` <thead> `  ,  ` <tbody> `  ,  ` <tr> `  ,  ` <th> `  ,  ` <td> ` 
    
    ** Good practice **  : The viewport  ` meta `  tag is considered an standard part of any HTML document and is required for pages to render correctly on mobile devices.   Without it, mobile browsers will render the page at a desktop-width viewport and then scale it down, making text unreadable.   Tables should be divided into a heading row (a  ` <thead> `  with a  ` <tr> `  element and nested  ` <th> `  header column elements) and data rows (a  ` <tbody> `  with one or more  ` <tr> `  elements with nested  ` <td> `  datum column elements). 
    

##   Generating bitmap images for web pages 

 Up to this    point, you have been working with image files that    already exist.   In real projects, you often need images before you have a designer, a photo library, or final assets. 

 Image generation tools are useful for this purpose especially as placeholders. 

 Tools such as Google’s Nano Banana and ChatGPT Images can generate bitmap images from text descriptions.   You can use them to create: 

*    Placeholder images while building your layout 
*    Hero images for landing pages 
*    Illustrations for blog posts or product pages 
*    Simple icons or visual accents 

 This gives you something to design around before the final artwork exists. 

 On April 21, 2026, OpenAI announced ChatGPT Images 2.0 with many improvements:  [  https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-images-2-0/  ](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-images-2-0/)

 The images    generated by these tools are usually bitmap images, meaning    they are made of pixels. 

 Common bitmap formats include: 

*    JPEG is good for photos 
*    PNG is good for transparency and sharp edges 
*    WebP is a format with good compression 

 When you are building a page layout, you often just need something that looks reasonable. 

 For example, you might prompt an image generator with: 

```
Please create a simple hero image with a soft blue gradient background, abstract shapes, clean and minimal, suitable for a tech website.
```

 The result does not need to be perfect.   It just needs to fill the space to give the page visual structure and help you think about layout and spacing.   This is much better than leaving empty space or using a broken image link. 

 A hero image is the large visual at the top of a page.   It sets the tone for everything that follows. 

 For example, for a survey app landing page, you might generate something like: 

```
Please create a web app hero image showing a dashboard with charts and polls, clean UI, light background, friendly colors, no text.
```

 A few practical tips for hero images: 

*    Avoid putting important text in the image itself; use real HTML text instead 
*    Keep the composition simple, so it works at different screen sizes 
*    Prefer wide, horizontal images for hero sections 

 Generated images are useful but remember that generated images can sometimes include visual artifacts or odd details.   Look at them critically before using them. 

 Bitmap images are not always the best choice.   For diagrams, icons, and anything that needs to scale cleanly or animate, vector graphics are usually better. 

 In  [* Chapter 4 *](#04.xhtml#_idTextAnchor212)  ,  * Drawing Scalable Graphics *  , you will learn about SVG, which is better than bitmaps for diagrams, charts, icons, animations, and dynamic graphics that change with data.   In this book’s survey project, SVG will be especially useful for rendering charts and visualizing results. 

 Use generated images to support the page, not to distract from it.   A useful image fits the content, the layout, and the purpose of the page.

 While the preview is open: 

*    Change the  ` <h1> `  and  ` <title> `  text to something else 
*    Add a new list item:  ` <li>I can preview changes instantly</li> `
*    Edit the table by changing a time value from 10 to 15 

 You’ve created a basic web page and used lots of different HTML elements.   You could create a full website with read-only content but it would be static.   One of the most common ways to make a website interactive is to provide forms for a visitor to fill in and then submit.   These could be login forms for authenticating a visitor, or forms to create or edit data. 

 Let’s look at how you can create web pages with forms and various input elements. 

#   Working with forms and inputs 

 So far, your page has    been  * read-only *  .   Forms are how a user types information into a page and sends it somewhere, like a    contact form, login screen, newsletter signup, checkout, and so on. 

 At the center of this is the  ` <form> `  element, which wraps your input controls (text boxes, dropdowns, buttons) and defines how the browser should submit the data. 

 In this section, you’re going to: 

1.   Create a new page called  ` contact.html `  with a contact form 
2.   Link to it from your  ` index.html ` ** About Me **  page 

##   Create contact.html 

 In VS Code, create a new file in the    same folder as  ` index.html `  :  ` contact.html `  . 

 Paste this in: 

 This HTML file is available from the following link:  [  https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/contact.html  ](https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/contact.html)

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Contact Me</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Contact Me</h1>
    <p>
      Use this form to send me a message. For now, it doesn't actually send email.
      It demonstrates how forms collect data and submit it to a server.
    </p>
    <form action="/contact" method="post">
      <h2>Your details</h2>
      <p>
        <label for="fullName">Full name</label><br>
        <input type="text" id="fullName" name="fullName" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="email">Email address</label><br>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="phone">Phone (optional)</label><br>
        <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone">
      </p>
      <h2>Your message</h2>
      <p>
        <label for="topic">Topic</label><br>
        <select id="topic" name="topic">
          <option value="question">Question</option>
          <option value="feedback">Feedback</option>
          <option value="business">Business inquiry</option>
        </select>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="message">Message</label><br>
        <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="6" cols="40" required></textarea>
      </p>
      <h2>Preferences</h2>
      <p>
        Preferred contact method:
        <br>
        <input type="radio" id="contactEmail" name="preferredContact" value="email" checked>
        <label for="contactEmail">Email</label>
        <br>
        <input type="radio" id="contactPhone" name="preferredContact" value="phone">
        <label for="contactPhone">Phone</label>
      </p>
      <p>
        <input type="checkbox" id="newsletter" name="newsletter" value="yes">
        <label for="newsletter">Send me occasional updates</label>
      </p>
      <p>
        <button type="submit">Send message</button>
        <button type="reset">Clear form</button>
      </p>
    </form>
    <p>
      <a href="index.html">Back to About Me</a>
    </p>
  </body>
</html>
```

 A few things to    notice: 

*    The  ` <form> `  has  ` action="/contact" `  and  ` method="post" ` 
    *   ` action `  is the URL the browser sends the form data to 
    *   ` method="post" `  sends the data in the request body;  ` get `  (the default) appends it to the URL after  ` ? `
*    Every control that should be submitted has a  ` name="..." `  .   If you forget name, the value won’t be included in the submitted data. 
*    Each text field is    labeled using  ` <label for="..."> `  that matches the input’s  ` id `  .   This improves both usability and accessibility. 

##   Link to the contact form from index.html 

 Open your existing  ` index.html `  and add a link    somewhere sensible, for example, under    your  ` Useful link `  section or near the bottom. 

 For example: 

```
<h2>Contact</h2>
<p>
  Want to get in touch?
  <a href="contact.html">Go to my contact form</a>.
</p>
```

 Because  ` contact.html `  is in the same folder as  ` index.html `  , a simple  ** relative link **  like    just the HTML filename works.   Alternatively, you could specify an  ** absolute link **  using a full URL:  ` https://example.com/contact.html `  . 

 An absolute link    is the full address of a resource, like a web page, that works regardless of the current page’s location.   A relative link is a shorter address based on the current page’s location.   If I am in Alaska and I want to send a letter to someone in Scotland, I would need to use their full, or absolute, address.   If I wanted to send a letter to someone on my street, I could hand it to a neighbor and ask them to give it to “Bob at number 23.”   This is their address relative to another address on the same street.   To send it to someone in the same city, we might need to use their street name too.   To send it to someone in the same state, we would need to include their city name as well.   A resource like a web page has one absolute address, and many relative addresses depending on how close you already are to their location.

 What you’ll likely    see right now:

##   A quick, practical table of common form elements 

 A cheat sheet you can keep nearby while learning is shown in  * Table 2.1 *  : 

 
| ** Element ** || ** Example ** || ** What it’s for ** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ` <form> ` || ` <form `` action="/contact" `` method="post"> ` ||  Wraps    inputs and defines where and how data is submitted.  ` action `  and  ` method `  control submission.  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ` <label> ` || ` <label for="email"> `` Email `` </label> ` ||  Provides a human-readable label for a form control.   Best practice is matching  ` for `  to the input’s  ` id `  .  |
| ` <input `` type="text"> ` || ` <input `` type="text" `` name="fullName"> ` ||  Single-line text input.   Include  ` name `  so it submits.  |
| ` <input `` type="email"> ` || ` <input type="email" `` name="email"> ` ||  Email-shaped input with basic validation in many browsers.  |
| ` <input `` type="tel"> ` || ` <input type="tel" `` name="phone"> ` ||  Phone number input (often shows a phone keypad on mobile).  |
| ` <textarea> ` || ` <textarea name="message"> `` </textarea> ` ||  Multi-line text input (great for messages).  |
| ` <select> + <option> ` || ` <select> `` <option value="..."> `` ...</option> `` ... `` </select> ` ||  Dropdown list of options.   Each has text inside and an optional  ` value `  .  |
| ` <input `` type="radio"> ` || ` <input type="radio" `` name="preferredContact" `` value="email"> ` ||  Choose one option from a group.   Grouping is done by sharing the same  ` name `  .  |
| ` <input `` type="checkbox"> ` || ` <input type="checkbox" `` name="newsletter" `` value="yes"> ` ||  On/off option (checked or unchecked).  |
| ` <button `` type="submit"> ` || ` <button type="submit"> `` Send</button> ` ||  Submits the form.  |
| ` <button `` type="reset"> ` || ` <button type="reset"> `` Clear</button> ` ||  Resets    fields to their initial values.  |

 Table 2.1: Common form elements 

 You’ll see lots more input types out there, but if a beginner gets comfortable with this set, they can build most basic forms. 

##   What “posting back to the web server” means 

 When the user clicks the  ** Send **  button, the browser takes all the form controls that have a  ` name `  and sends them as an HTTP request to the URL in the action. 

 There are two common ways to    submit the data: 

*   ` GET `  (default): the form    data is appended to the URL after ?   This is good for searches and filters where you want a shareable URL. 
*   ` POST `  : the form data is    sent in the request body.   This is common for contact forms, logins, or anything that changes server state, like a form for editing customer or order data. 

 On the server side (you’ll do this later with Django), your web app would: 

1.   Receive the request at something like  ` /contact `
2.   Read the submitted fields (name/value pairs) 
3.   Validate them (for real, not just browser validation) 
4.   Do something useful:  
    *    Store it in a database 
    *    Send an email 
    *    Create a support ticket 
5.   Return a response page (like  ** Thanks, message received! **  ) 

 At this stage, you’re only building the HTML user interface.   Server-side processing comes later. 

** Prompt **  : Please show what form data looks like when it is submitted from a browser including the difference between  ` GET `  and  ` POST `  with real HTTP examples.

 While HTML specializes in web content, it is just one of several markup languages, and understanding related technologies like XML and SVG helps round out how structured data and graphics are represented on the web.   Let’s learn about those languages next. 

#   Other markup languages 

 HTML is the markup language most closely associated with the web, but it belongs to a wider family of languages that use tags to describe content.   Understanding this family will help you see that HTML isn’t random or magical.   It’s one practical solution that emerged from a longer history. 

##   What “markup language” means 

 A  ** markup language **  is a    system for adding annotations to text so that a computer can understand what different parts of that text represent.   In other words, markup answers questions like: 

*    Is this text a heading or a paragraph? 
*    Is this a list item or a table cell? 
*    Is this content data, structure, or metadata? 

 Markup languages do not execute logic.   They describe structure and meaning.   That puts HTML in the same conceptual category as languages like XAML and SVG. 

 HTML    is a domain-specific markup language designed for one job: describing documents meant to be viewed in a web browser. 

 HTML is intentionally forgiving.   Browsers try very hard to display something sensible even if the markup is imperfect.   That design choice is one of the reasons the web spread so quickly. 

** XML **  (  ** eXtensible Markup Language **  ) came    later and took a different approach.   Where HTML is opinionated and forgiving, XML is strict about syntax, extensible (you define your own tags), and focused on data, not presentation. 

 An example of XML is shown in the following code: 

```
<book>
  <title>Python Programming</title>
  <author>Mark</author>
  <pages>320</pages>
</book>
```

 There are some key differences between XML and HTML: 

*    Every tag must be closed either with a closing tag (  ` <book>...</book> `  ) or as a self-closing tag (  ` <br /> `  ) because, unlike HTML5, which allows unclosed void elements, XML will not allow them 
*    Tags must be properly nested 
*    There is no predefined set of tags 
*    XML does not define how things should look 

 XML is commonly used for configuration files, data interchange, document formats, and APIs (especially historically). 

** Prompt **  : Please explain why HTML is forgiving but XML is strict, with examples. 

##   SVG: markup for graphics 

** SVG **  (  ** Scalable Vector Graphics **  ) is    another markup language, but for graphics instead of documents.   SVG uses tags to describe shapes, paths, text, and transformations, as shown in the following code: 

```
<svg width="100" height="100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" />
</svg>
```

 There are important things to understand about SVG: 

*    It is XML-based 
*    It describes  * what the graphic is *  , not how to draw pixels 
*    It scales cleanly at any resolution 

 SVG can be embedded directly inside HTML documents, which is why learning HTML structure makes SVG easier to understand later.   You will learn about SVG in  [* Chapter 4 *](#04.xhtml#_idTextAnchor212) * , SVG – Drawing Scalable Graphics *  . 

##   A very short history of markup languages 

 HTML was not the first    markup language: 

1.   Early document systems    based on  ** Standard Generalized Markup Language **  (  ** SGML **  ) inspired structured markup long before the web.   It is the grandparent of most markup languages, including HTML, XML, and anything derived from them.   SGML is a meta-language, not a markup language in the everyday sense.   That means SGML does not define a fixed set of tags.   Instead, it defines rules for creating your own markup languages. 
2.   HTML    was created to describe scientific documents with links.   As browsers became more powerful, and became important for commerce and industry, HTML grew features.   HTML is an SGML application. 
3.   XML    emerged to provide a strict, general-purpose markup format.   XML is a simplified descendant of SGML. 
4.   SVG    emerged to describe graphics in a resolution-independent way.   SVG inherits SGML ideas via XML. 
5.  ** XAML **  (  ** Extensible Application Markup Language **  ) is a    markup language created by Microsoft for defining user interfaces in desktop and cross-platform applications, rather than web pages.   XAML is most commonly    used with  ** WPF **  (  ** Windows Presentation Foundation **  ), WinUI, .NET MAUI, and Avalonia. 

 They are not competitors.   They are variations on the same idea: structured markup with meaning, applied to different domains. 

** Prompt **  : Where does XHTML fit in the history of markup languages? 

##   Why beginners should care 

 HTML is not unique because it uses tags.   It’s unique because it uses markup to describe documents meant for the web.   Other markup languages exist for other jobs. 

 HTML just happens to be the one that holds the web together. 

 SGML is not something you learn to use.   It is something you learn about.   It’s the root of the markup family tree.   Everything else makes more sense once you know where it came from. 

#   References and resources 

 Let’s review the official HTML documentation and references. 

##   MDN web docs (beginners should start here) 

 MDN Web Docs is    the best HTML documentation on the internet for learning and day-to-day reference.   It is maintained by Mozilla with contributions from browser vendors and the web community. 

*    Homepage:  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/%20)
*    HTML overview:  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML%20)
*    HTML elements reference:  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element%20)
*    Forms and input elements:  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Forms  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Forms)  ,  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/form  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/form)  , and  [  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input  ](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input%20)

 MDN is so good because it is written for humans, not lawyers, with uncomplicated examples, and it explains why, not just what.   It is kept in sync with real browser behavior. 

** Good practice **  : If a beginner uses only one documentation site while learning HTML, it should be MDN. 

##   W3C HTML specification (official but not beginner friendly) 

 The  ** World Wide Web Consortium **  (  ** W3C **  ) publishes the    official HTML specifications.   This is the formal definition of how HTML works at a standards level. 

*    HTML specification landing    page:  [  https://www.w3.org/TR/html/  ](https://www.w3.org/TR/html/%20)
*    Living HTML    standard (WHATWG, see below):  [  https://html.spec.whatwg.org/  ](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/%20)

 The specification is written for browser implementers like the programmers at Microsoft, Google, and Apple, who build rendering engines.   It is not written to teach HTML.   It is dense, precise, and unforgiving. 

 This is reference material, not learning material.   You don’t read it cover to cover.   You look things up when you need exact behavior. 

##   WHATWG HTML living standard 

 Most browsers now    follow the WHATWG HTML Living Standard, which evolves continuously instead of being frozen into versions. 

 HTML Living    Standard:  [  https://html.spec.whatwg.org/  ](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/%20)

 For current browser behavior, this is the main specification to check. 

 Again, this is not beginner reading.   It’s for checking edge cases, resolving ambiguity, and understanding how browsers really behave. 

##   How beginners should actually use these resources 

 A practical approach is to start with MDN, build a small example, and consult the specification only when needed: 

*    Concepts 
*    Examples 
*    Best practices 

 Then get your hands dirty by building something: 

*    Make mistakes 
*    Break things 
*    Fix them 

 Only then glance at the official specifications if: 

*    Browser behavior seems odd 
*    You need absolute precision 
*    You’re curious how the machinery works 

 For learning HTML, use MDN Web Docs.   It explains HTML the way humans think. 

 The W3C and WHATWG specifications define how browsers work, but they are not teaching material.   Treat them as reference manuals, not tutorials. 

#   Summary 

 In this chapter, you learned the following: 

*    HTML describes the structure and meaning of content, not how it looks 
*    An HTML document is built from elements, which are made of tags and content 
*    Attributes provide additional information that configures how elements behave 
*    Headings create a logical outline of a page and should reflect meaning, not appearance 
*    Paragraphs, lists, links, images, and tables represent different types of content 
*    Elements can be nested to form a hierarchical structure that browsers interpret as a tree 
*    Block-level elements structure layout, while inline elements flow within text 
*    Semantic HTML improves accessibility, search engine understanding, and maintainability 
*    Forms allow users to input data and submit it to a server using  ` GET `  or  ` POST `
*    Every form control must have a name to be included in submitted data 
*    HTML is forgiving and designed for documents, unlike stricter markup languages like XML 
*    SVG uses markup to describe scalable graphics and can be embedded in HTML 
*    Good HTML creates a strong starting point for CSS styling and JavaScript interactivity 

 In the next chapter, you will learn about CSS, a language used to provide styling and layout to the content on a web page.
